  "text": "Every Thursday, the sea returned something it had taken.

Usually it was a sandal, a fishing float, a crate with foreign lettering. Once, it was a piano stool.

Elias kept a ledger in the coastguard hut. He recorded each object, where it had washed ashore, and who came to claim it.

He had been doing this for thirty-one years when the sea returned his father's watch.

He knew the dent beside the winding stem. He had made it himself, dropping the watch onto the kitchen tiles while pretending to be late for work.

His father had laughed.

That was the part Elias had forgotten.

He carried the watch home in his coat pocket. All evening he expected it to tick, though its hands were missing and the glass was clouded white.

On Friday, a boy knocked at the hut.

“My gran says you found a watch.”

Elias closed the ledger.

“Lots of watches get lost.”

“She says this one's got a dent.”

The boy produced a photograph. An old woman stood beside Elias's father on a promenade Elias did not recognize. His father wore the watch.

“When was this taken?” Elias asked.

The boy turned it over. The date was twelve years after the funeral.

Outside, the tide dragged pebbles down the beach.

“My gran can't manage the steps,” the boy said. “She's waiting in the car.”

Elias reached for his coat, then stopped and took the watch from its pocket.

He left the ledger open. In the space reserved for the claimant's name, he had written his own.

He crossed it out before going downstairs."
